maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
I find myself in accord, generally speaking, with the statements of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and also, with one or two exceptions, of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I wish to deal chiefly with statements that were made in the earlier part of the debate and with one or two that were made prior to the debate.
I was much interested in some observations of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on the subject of relief, and I was somewhat disturbed when these ministers stated that in their opinion the only money that could be made available for relief was the money that the government could tax from the pockets of the people. It seems very strange that such statements should come from members of a government elected on a platform of monetary reform. It seems even stranger that the Minister of Labour should make the statement that if the federal government were to assume the responsibility for all relief it would be necessary to increase taxation against the incomes of the people in the lower brackets, and also perhaps to raise the sales tax, which falls heaviest upon the poorer classes of people. Perhaps it would have been a good thing if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had taken one or two of these ministers with him on the election campaign, so that after he had soared high, wide and handsome in the realms of monetary reform it would have been possible for the Minister of Labour to get up and bring people back to earth by telling them that the only way the Liberal party could make money available to meet the domestic and social requirements of the people was by increasing taxation against the poorer classes. Had that statement been made during the elections I should not have been criticizing the government to-day. But not

only was that statement not made, but there echoed from one end of Canada to the other the Prime Minister's statements telling the people how currency and credit would be made available in terms of public need, showing how money would be available to meet the domestic and social requirements of the Canadian people.
The other day when the Minister of Finance was spealdng and praising the policy of the Bank of Canada, he said the bank had made money available for the industrial requirements of the people. But there was no word said as to "social" and "domestic" requirements, words that were spoken so freely in speeches prior to the election.
I listened with great interest to the essay read by the Minister of Finance, but it was largely spoiled for me owing to the fact that in the latter part of it there was a large number of misstatements of facts and a large number of false charges against ourselves that cannot be substantiated by the minister. With those statements I shall deal a little later.
The Minister of Finance criticized the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) because he quoted somewhat freely from certain authors who are not believers in social credit. The hon. member never at any time quoted those authors as supporters of social credit; he quoted them as supporting certain principles which are fundamentals of social credit. I would also point out that whenever the hon. member for Lethbridge quoted these gentlemen he named the author, the title of the book, and the page on which the quotations could be found. When the Minister of Finance attributed statements to Major Douglas and ourselves and other social crediters he did noi on a single occasion give the name of the book or the place where the quotations could be found. When the hon. member for Lethbridge challenged him and asked where the statements could be found, the Minister of Finance merely stated that he had read many books and these were his general impressions. I challenge the Minister of Finance to show where those statements can be found. I shall be referring to them later on.
Our motion points out that there is poverty in Canada and states that in our opinion the government is not taking the necessary steps to remove that poverty by adequately developing our natural resources. It is true that there has been a partial recovery in Canada, largely due to the fact that the world to-day is spending millions upon millions on armaments. In the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I read from a letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce which makes that very clear. In order to

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
obtain a proper perspective of conditions in Canada to-day I should like to draw a rough picture. On the one side we have a great productive plant working at only a small percentage of its capacity. We have abundant natural resources barely touched, tremendous sources of energy which can be developed, a large surplus of labour unemployed, and many who are working only part time. On the other side we see a sordid picture; a great army of people on the verge of starvation, about 900,000 on relief, and many thousands more whose standard of living is insufficient to provide the requirements of a healthy existence. Are not the people fully justified, then, in asking why in a Christian democracy it is not possible to employ that surplus labour in factories and industries that are working only part time, in order to produce from our wealth of natural resources goods which are so sorely needed by these starving masses? Is it a problem beyond the power of the government or of man to solve?
We have heard hon. members state that this condition of things is the fault of industry; they blame industry for not expanding. But how can industry expand when there is not a market for its goods? We have stressed time and again the reason why it cannot be done. We have shown why there is no effective market. The physical demand is there, but of what use is it unless it can be made effective?-and it can be made effective only by putting money in the pockets of those who need the goods. I have shown that it cannot be done unless you have a sufficient volume of capital production to pay out wages to restore the balance. I have pointed out that there must be a certain relationship between the production of consumption goods and of capital goods. I was therefore surprised when the Minister of Finance stated, as reported at page 1156 of Hansard:
Another error which the social erediters make is to overlook entirely the fact that consumers do not buy the whole product of industry. A very substantial proportion of the total product of industry consists of producers' or capital goods-machinery, tools, equipment, etc-which never come into the hands of consumers and which they never have to buy. The firms which are producing these capital goods pay wages, salaries and dividends which constitute purchasing power in the hands of consumers for the purchase of consumers' goods produced by other industries. It is therefore absurd to contend that sufficient money could be placed in the hands of consumers to enable them to purchase the entire produce of industry.
The Minister of Finance states that consumers are not required to pay for capital goods. Does he suggest that the owners of the factories of Canada to-day are philanthropists. allowing their factories to be used 51952-83
to produce goods without charging for the use of the factories? When goods are produced in a factory, included in the price of those goods will be a certain charge to cover the cost of equipping and maintaining the factory. Therefore unquestionably consumers not only pay for consumers' goods but also their share of the cost of depreciation of the plant that produced those goods.
I have spoken on this subject several times in the house, and every time I have referred to the fact that industry cannot create its own demand unless there is a sufficient volume of capital goods produced so that the salaries and wages paid in their production will be equal to the deficiency that exists as between the effective demand of the people and the total price of the goods available for distribution. I stressed that fact the first time I spoke and on other occasions since then, yet the minister says we have always ignored that point. I am not blaming the minister for not listening to or reading our speeches, I know he is a busy man, but I think he should be a little more accurate than to make such a sweeping statement.
So we have said it is necessary to issue additional money or purchasing power outside of the industrial system in order to make up this deficiency. When we make that statement, it is claimed that such action would cause inflation. What is inflation? The hon. member for Lethbridge dealt with this subject at some length, so I shall touch on it only briefly. Inflation to a very large extent depends on the relationship between the aggregate of prices of desired goods available for distribution and the total effective demand of the people. In other words, if the total price of desired goods available for distribution was $2,000 and the total effective demand of the people was S2,000, the two would balance and there would be stabilization. If, on the other hand, the effective demand was increased to $2,500 and there was no increase in production, unquestionably you would have inflation; the price of goods would rise to absorb that surplus money. But if when demand increased from S2,000 to $2,500 production were stepped up to the same amount you would again have stabilization. Carl Snyder, chief statistician of the federal reserve banks of America, has pointed out, by a series of charts showing the relationship between volume of credit and volume of production over a long period of time, that so long as the volume of credit parallels the volume of production there is no variation in the price level. In other words, by dividing your volume of credit by the volume of production you find the price level at

After listening to the social credit explanations I am not very much surprised that Mr. Aber-hart suggested the heed for calling in experts. At Cooking Lake last year he said:
The people need not bother how these aims (the aims of social credit) might be accomplished-leave that to the experts chosen to do it. Don't let details bother you, ask for results. For goodness sake don't get an inferiority complex. You cannot get anything if you don't think you can get it. How? That is something you don't need to bother about. You go ahead with your farm work.
But the thing that puzzled me this afternoon as I listened to these speeches was why it was necessary to go abroad for assistance when we have such experts in this house. My hon. friend has suggested that dividends can be paid; that there is a surplus from which production can be distributed, but I am rather curious and I should like to get the advice of these experts. I think it is more than probable that during the last two or three years consumption has actually exceeded production in Alberta. When we calculate consumption in that sense we must take into account depreciation in the value of equipment and machinery which has not been maintained during the depression. The whole province has allowed its equipment to run down and deteriorate. Perhaps we have an explanation for Mr. Aberhart not coming through with his dividends. Dividends would have to be paid out of surplus, and it may be that after examination by his experts it was found that there was no surplus to be distributed. If he had been compelled to attempt the task, the only thing he could have given was a dividend in reverse; that is, the people residing in that province would have had to contribute to the state instead of the state contributing something to them.
The essence of the story presented by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), amounts to this:
We are producing goods but people cannot buy them. Why cannot people buy the goods produced and how can we manage so that the people will be enabled to buy?
The contention of my hon. friend is the basic contention of the party to which he belongs. I do not accept that statement in the form in which it is presented; yet I think as it stands it deserves careful analysis. There is something wrong with our method of distribution when we find ourselves in the difficulties that confront us to-day, but I cannot follow their argument. I hold in my hand a book. Let us assume that it cost me $2 when I bought it from the store. I gave the storekeeper S2 and that $2 means purchasing

power as far as he is concerned. He pays the wholesaler for the book; the wholesaler pays the publisher and the publisher distributes what he receives in the form of costs. Right back to the end of the line these costs are distributed.

Would you say that if
you bought the book at cost there would be a profit?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
The profit would go
back into purchasing power. Suppose the man from whom I purchased the book makes fifty cents, on it. He can turn around and buy something from me in exchange if I have something to sell. The cost is, beyond question, distributed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) used boots as an example the other night. Take whichever example you choose; in no way has there been a loss of purchasing power. When you buy a product, you pay for it and when you pay for it, you pay something which is purchasing power. Let me put it to my hon. friend in this way. Go back to the old days of barter. Instead of paying for that book with a two dollar bill, I pay for it with two bushels of wheat. The two bushels of wheat would buy something else, would it not? I cannot understand how there can be any possibility of misunderstanding in a simple transaction like this. You cannot find out, at least I have never been able to find a social crediter who could explain where the missing item was or where it had gone to. Is it up their sleeves? To find it is like looking in a dark room for a black cat that is not there. There is no possibility of its being there.
There is another aspect that deserves serious consideration. I refer to the picture presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The hon. member asserted that there was to-day a maldistribution of purchasing power in the Dominion of Canada and in practically every country of the world. I should like to give some facts which have been brought out by the Brookings Institution, which has been quoted quite often in the house. The findings of this institution are a direct challenge to the economic thought of the age. It is true the essential points are not new; they have been stated and restated in a hundred different forms; but Doctor Moulton has presented them in direct relationship to the needs of to-day. The figures given deal with the United States, but I shall give the Canadian figures later on. He said:
Families getting less than $1,250, in the average, saved nothing in 1929.

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
That is in the United States. I think that is a rational conclusion.
Out of $15,000,000,000 of individual savings $13,000,000,000 were made by ten per cent of the population in the higher income classes. As a greater proportion of families moved into these classes over a period of years, a greater proportion of money income was saved. Only part of this went to build new plant.
In the past when I heard that statement I would have answered: Well, what is the matter? I would have said that this saving goes into the banks, and the banks lend the money. I would have said it goes for the purchase of bonds, the bonds of manufacturing establishments, or railways, or whatever it might be, and that again would go back into producing more purchasing power and giving employment to people. But we have to consider these things in the light of conditions as they are to-day. When business is active and accumulated funds seek productive investment, that would be true. In the conditions which existed in 1929, that would be true. But for some reason to-day, under different conditions, that does not follow, and I am now going to give the house figures which show how much has drifted into the form of bonds held by the banks of Canada, and how much is not being used of the available credit which might be used in the Dominion of Canada.
What do we find? Current loans and discounts of banks in Canada stood at 81,343,000,000 for the year 1929. Business-was using the available credit at that time. The level was $731,000,000 on December 31, 1937, a decline of S600,000,000.

What is the significance of these facts? We are not using our available credit for production. Savings are going into bonds and securities. Money is seeking a safe harbour. It is seeking a safe harbour because of fear, because of the situation which exists in the world to-day; and of course, being faithful to the cause I
represent, I must contend that it is in part due to mistakes of government, perhaps even in part of this government.
I have here the report of income tax collections for 1936. It shows that 199,102 people paid income tax. In 1931 the total number of people gainfully employed was 3.927,230. Assuming that the number gainfully employed was the same in 1936 as in 1931- and the difference would not be large-we have 3,728,128 who came below the income tax levels. Of those who paid income tax 175,492 were in the bracket of $5,000 or less, and contributed a total of $4,204,731. The remaining 23,610 paid more than $28,000,000. When you pay your income tax, and your income is ten or twenty or fifty thousand dollars, I venture to suggest that in the great majority of cases it goes back not into consumer goods but into investments, into bonds or savings. While it might in normal times, or would in normal times, be employed in the production of capital goods it does not now go back into the production of capital goods because money is invested in capital goods for the production of consumer goods, and if there is no demand for consumer goods then money will not flow in capital production.
In Canada our population is more largely rural than in the United States. There is practically no saving so far as the farmers are concerned, so that we would have a larger number of people with small incomes on which they were incapable of saving in the normal course of events, and the savings which have been accumulated have been accumulated largely among the more favoured class.

thousand dollar income people are not included.

Yes, I recognize that. We have now this situation. There is unquestionably at the present time (1) maldistribution of income; (2) wealth, savings, credit power concentrated in the hands of relatively few; (3) a decline in the use of credit for industry. The capital goods market is at a low level.
In essence, therefore, we have a situation which is almost unique in Canadian history. The market for capital goods is not sufficient to absorb our excess production. There was a net capital export from the Dominion of Canada during the past year: that is, we bought back some of our production from abroad because there was not a good market for capital investment in this country.
In the past our periods of prosperity have been followed by a succession of depressions

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
and booms. The idea occurs to me that while each successive boom actually rose to a higher level than the preceding boom and brought about a higher standard of living and more comfort to many people, we may now be reaching the point where there may be a recession in these peaks and I sometimes raise the question in my own mind whether we may not for some time to come fail to reach a peak as high as we have reached during the past boom. There are certain things which indicate this. Intensive nationalism such as has developed throughout the world calls for lower standards of living. I do not think there is anyone here so stem an advocate of protection and of the doctrine of exclusion that he would deny the assertion that when each little nation is cribbed, cabined and confined within its own narrow boundaries, the standard of living is not going to be as high as it would be in normal times. Second, we have rigid control of industry. We have fixed prices. There is so much of the economic area which is fixed that those who are outside the field of privilege, that is the farmer, the basic producers generally and the common labourer, are on a very low level, and they must have a difficult position during any period in which business is not above its normal level. Third, a highly mechanized industry produces at a low cost when it is running at 100 per cent level of activity; but when mechanized industry begins to produce in a period of depression, when the steel industry in the United States, for example, is down at a level of approximately 26, that is high cost production, and it means high costs in selling and high cost for its consumers. When these high costs are reached it is extremely difficult for the men in the lower income brackets to be able to buy back the goods which are produced, because they have no real purchasing power.
I say this further-and here is where I shall get into difficulty with the hon. member for Rosthern who, I am sorry, is not with me. I am not sure that we can solve all these problems by the new method of playing with the counters. We are now to have managed currency. Managed currency has to be managed by men. Men are capable of making mistakes, just as well as the old form of currency was capable of wrong use. But there is this that can be said of the gold standard, that at least it kept its word so long as men did not make it impossible for it to keep its word. The problem we have to-day is not so much to play with the money we have as

to get goods exchanged and to develop markets, and this is a problem which we are not facing when we turn our sole attention to the problem of money.
Now what is to be done? The capital goods market has been more or less destroyed. There is maldistribution. Consumptive demand is insufficient. In the United States they have developed a certain solution or attempted solution of this particular problem. It is the great and glorious pastime of "soaking the rich." They have also tried the other method of expanding the demand for credit and money by means of government expenditures. Well, I suppose I have the right to differ from some of my friends in this corner of the house. The hon. member for Rosthern suggests that highways can be built and other large government enterprises undertaken. But I suggest that that involves the production of something which must have an exchange value equal to its cost of production; otherwise it is not profitable to the community as a whole to have it produced. For if the people of Canada have to be taxed to build a road to a park in northern Saskatchewan-and I am not singling that out for distinction as not being a good place to build a road; the same reasoning would apply if they had to pay taxes to build a road into Huron county-if they are to pay taxes for the building of a road, it must be because the Canadian people feel, that that road has an exchange value equivalent to its cost of production; in other words, that the Canadian people as a whole or the people of some community in Canada will be able to exchange the product which they produce for the benefit of having that road where it is.

I am in no doubt so far as that is concerned. We may put up beautiful

buildings and fine monuments, and they have a value; but when the government expends money upon 'the construction of a public building it is an entirely different matter from spending it upon a business enterprise. If we build a new post office in Ottawa, does it increase the payroll? Will there be more stamps sold? Will more money orders be bought? We may operate more efficiently in a new and better equipped post office, but it will do very little to add to the production of wealth in Canada.

When the house took recess at six o'clock I had pointed out that in the United States they had tried a number of different means to restore prosperity, but despite these attempts the United States today seems to hold the lead in the drift into another depression. Some time ago the Natural Resources Committee in the United States made a report on the development of industry in that country. A summary of their finding appeared in the Index published by the New York Trust Company in November last. The investigation covered manufacturing, mining, steam railways and telephonic communication. I give you only one illustration, that of manufacturing. Taking 100 as representing the volume of output in 1920, production in 1934 stood at 94. The man hours required in 1920 for that year's production being shown by the index number of 100, the man hours required for the production of the reduced volume of 1934 were 52. This gives us a figure of approximately 56 for the man hours required to produce 100 units of goods in 1934 in comparison with 100 man hours for production of the same volume of goods in 1920.
I want to make that point clear. It took approximately fifty-six per cent of the number of man hours to produce the volume of goods in 1934 which was produced by 100 man hours or units of work in 1920. Measure what that means in volume of unemployment, if nothing else occurs to alter that movement. I admit at once that there are variations in the kinds of production between 1920 and 1934; also there are variations in the means of distribution. I admit that other factors may operate to relieve the volume of unemployment resulting from that decrease in man power required. But I want to ask the house just one question: If that number of men
can be discharged from industry with the volume of production remaining practically the same, what becomes of the problem of employment in Canada and the United States unless some other adjustment is made?
Now what adjustment is necessary? Why is machinery installed? Machinery is put in because it will reduce the labour cost of the product. No manufacturer instals new machinery unless he believes that by doing so the number of men required to operate his factory can be reduced. I do not suggest for a moment that if the free play of natural forces were allowed to operate, that would mean, over the long period, a reduction of employment. But if there is something which enables the manufacturer, after dismissing these men, to continue to sell his goods at the same price, then there is unemployment, and the next step is to throw the burden of that unemployment upon the state. The only remedy as far as I can see is that the price be permitted to fall in order that there may be enlarged purchasing power, and the increase in demand for goods, although it may not apply to this particular factory, expands into other divisions of production, because the desires of man are limitless; as long as he has purchasing power he will go on buying. That is the only way as far as I know by which that balance can be effected. But if on the other hand we are going to hold prices up; if we are going to have, as we have in Canada now, rules and restrictions of every possible kind tending against reductions in prices; if we are going to pile up tariffs; if we have obstructions which restrict imports like sections 36 and 43 in the Customs Act, then the inevitable follows. It makes no difference what speeches we make about these questions; it matters not what we do at election time; the thing that matters is what we do when we assemble here trying to govern this Dominion of Canada.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) who spoke this afternoon, is in entire accord with me, I think, in the analysis I have given so far. We have moved along somewhat parallel lines. But he proposes an entirely different remedy. His idea, as expressed this afternoon, is that the government should take over the control of production and that we should move towards the socialist state. I fail to see how any man can hold that opinion in view of our knowledge of government efforts to-day in Canada and other countries. We have problems enough on our hands, with the hydro-electric development in Ontario, the Canadian National Railways, the operation of government owned utilities in different

provinces. It seems to me that if the solution is to be found along that line our progress must be very slow. We have to develop step by step the ability to walk, the ability indeed to stand upright and to move at all, before we go on to face the problem of the administration of the entire industrial life of the dominion. Think of the complexity of the problem of trying to organize production and distribution of all the multi-complex lines of production and distribution and services in Canada if we remove free initiative and say that all has to be planned by government.
Last year I read the record in the Saturday Evening Post of some United States engineers who were working in Russia. Their great difficulty was that they had to compile so many records and so much time was consumed in making reports to this division and that, and in the voluminous correspondence, that they had no time to go on with their work. By the time they had the reports finished and plans prepared and approved, the whole thing was so completely mixed that it was surprising that they ever reached the stage of production.
The only remedy I can see is to face the situation by a return to freedom, by removing the barriers and permitting the free play of natural forces. What is there to control production except price? When the price falls too low we cease to produce; when it goes up we return to production. There may be waste in that process; mistakes may be made, as they made mistakes in the United States a short time age when they tried to control production and ran into a period of scarcity. But after all, over a period of years, the only possible way by which you can reach a reasonable level of production and price is by the free play of natural forces.
In discussing this question the other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) came to what I think is a reasonably wise conclusion. I have noticed some criticism of the efforts of the government in the past few years, and sometimes I am free with that criticism myself. But I am wondering what the results would be if my hon. friends in the other corner were in power.

I wonder if it is not worse in Alberta. At least we have kept clear of some things in regard to which they are somewhat involved out there. If my social credit friends had absolute power in Canada I wonder if they would do any better or show any greater capacity for the direction of affairs

than they have shown in Alberta. I wonder, too, how my Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends would get along if they were directing affairs. One of my hon. friends remarks that things could not be worse. Well, in that connection there would be as much diversity of opinion as there sometimes is in this party, with perhaps no better sense of direction! My hon. friend the Minister of Finance made this remark:
Fundamentally our need is an actual increase in material wealth, not a different yardstick with which to measure it.
I agree with that, but it is not the only fundamental need. It requires the redistribution of the wealth now being created so that the relationship between savings and consumption shall be altered in accordance with the needs of to-day. Change the direction of savings and of investment; and again I say the only means by which that can be done is by free competition, by lowering the prices of goods and increasing consumption, thereby establishing demand. We may hold prices, but when we do volume drops. After all, the total measure of goods and services which we secure for our work is the result of two variables, price and volume, and if you hold the price at a high level the volume of consumption will be decreased. Therefore in terms of actual goods you will be poorer than you were before. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance also caught the vision of that need, and I hope he means to apply it. In his concluding paragraph he said:
Such an increase in material wealth can be best secured by facilitating the production of the many commodities which Canada is best adapted to produce, and by exchanging these products on as large a scale as possible for products which Canada cannot advantageously produce, receiving in return for our exports as much rather than as little as possible.
That is a delightful phrase. I might almost have written it myself, but the strange thing is that my hon. friends who hold out this admirable advice do not always follow it.
I referred to section 36 of the Customs Act. I want to read a word or two of that. This is a section of an act which is framed for the purpose of making goods cost more. It serves no other purpose. It reads:
The value for duty of new or unused goods shall in no case be less than the actual cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment direct to Canada plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit-
In other words, when we bring in goods from the United States we have a section of an act here which says that these goods shall be valued at a price which covers the cost of production and i\ reasonable selling cost, plus

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
a profit to the United States manufacturers. We are not to buy from United States sources unless we see that the United States manufacturer makes a profit. That is the essence of the story. Farmers in my constituency bought cattle last fall for six cents a pound. After feeding them all winter they will probably sell those cattle this spring for five and a quarter cents a pound, and there is not a word from either side of the house. Can you tell me what is the remedy? I do not know, but you ought not to insult these farmers by telling them that in the Customs Act there is a section which says that if they want to buy blue denim to make a pair of overalls they must be very careful to see that the United States manufacturer from whom they buy those goods is paid a price which allows him a reasonable profit. I wonder what would happen if one of my hon. friends, on either side of the house, were to employ a purchasing agent and send him out to buy goods. Would he give that agent a lecture first and say, "Buy where you like, but be sure that the man from whom you buy gets a profit." Yet that section remains part of the legislation of our country; it is in force, and was put into effect last year for what reason? It was done to prevent prices of cotton goods in Canada from being reduced, when they had fallen in the United States by virtue of the reduction in the price of raw cotton both in that country and in this.
That is what happened. That is the situation. We have legislation to keep up selling prices,' to make us pay more for material we buy, and the same sort of things runs all through the Customs Act. I have on my desk a letter which I received from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley); I am sorry he is not in the house. All it means is this, that a manufacturer in my own constituency bought some leather in the city of Chicago. A man was sent post-haste from Ottawa to Wingham in order to investigate that purchase-to see if the man paid too much for it? No; to see that he paid enough for it; to see that the price was sufficiently high, made so by government regulation, so that he would be compelled to charge a higher price for the gloves which he produced from that leather. When you face that situation; when you look at what we have done in regard to sugar, it makes you wonder. Under section 43 of the Customs Act we revalued sugar coming from Cuba at a price which took millions of dollars out of the pockets of the Canadian people.
We see the provisions contained in sections 43 and 36 of this act; we see this tariff
piled as high as it is to-day, after we have been in office for some time, and I say this is evidence that you are not recognizing the fundamental problem which faces us in this dominion to-day. Whether it is applied by the hon. gentlemen on this side of the house, I mean those separated from me spiritually but not physically; whether it is applied by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house, associated with me spiritually but separated physically, and differing sometimes quite widely in regard to the questions I am now discussing, or whether it is applied by hon. members in the far corner; no matter how it is done, for what cause or on what excuse, I say the sure, certain, inevitable result of that policy is to lay the foundations, not for the expansion of employment in Canada, but for the still further restriction of the employment-which we now have.
I appeal to you to-night to place this upon a reasonable basis. I am not making these statements merely to oppose somebody on this side or that.
In the debate of the last few days rve have been trying to find out the causes of these conditions, to seek a solution-as I asked that it should be sought the other day, when I said that debate should be nothing but a search for the truth. There is no desire on my part to challenge the attitude of any party, no matter upon what side they may be, so long as they make an effort towards the solution of this problem. Do we mean to say that 245 members of the House of Commons, who are trained in political life, trained in economics and with a vast experience, are going to close their eyes and say that the problem is impossible of solution-impossible of solution, because it is impossible for us to blaze a new trail; impossible of solution because we cannot do something which has not been done before; impossible of solution for one reason, and only one, namely, that we fail to realize that we must live in conformity with certain economic laws, sternly set, built in the veiy fabric of our lives? Believe me, you cannot escape obeying them without paying the price-and that price is unemployment, higher taxes, disruption of government and, far, far above that, the payment in terms of broken lives. For that is what we do when we break the economic laws by which we are governed, and which we ought to obey, if we are to find a solution and make life happier for the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since criticism has been directed against social credit, and since the founder of social credit is not here to speak for himself,

I would like to read a few quotations from the works of Major Douglas. He puts the root causes of our economic troubles as follows:
(1)	Wages, salaries and dividends will not purchase total production. This difficulty is cumulative.
(2)	The only sources of the purchasing power necessary to make up the difference are loan and export credits.
(3)	All industrial nations are competing for export credits. The end of that is war.
(4)	The major distribution of purchasing power to individuals, is through the media of wages and salaries. The preponderating factor in production is improving process of the utilization of solar energy.
(5)	This latter tends to displace wages and salaries, and the consequent distribution of the product to individuals. The credit factor in purchasing power thus increases in importance and dominates production.
(6)	This production is consequently of a character demanded by those in control of credit and is capital production.
(7)	The fundamental derivation of credit is from the community of individuals, and because -individuals are ceasing to benefit by its use it is breaking down.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat has said that the remedy is to lower prices, so as to cheapen production. I would like to read Major Douglas's answer to that. He is speaking of that very policy which was put into force by the British government a year or two after the end of the great war, at which time there was a cry of "produce more and consume less." They thought that by so doing they could save enough money to pay for the war. Douglas says this:
Consider now the policy actually being pursued at this moment by the government-
That is the British government.
-and the financial powers to deal with the problem. They can be summarized in one sentence-the reduction of costs, and more especially the labour costs. But labour costs are wages and form by far the most important item in the total purchasing power inside the country available for the distribution of goods. Even supposing that retail prices were reduced in exact ratio to wage reductions, which is highly improbable or even impossible, how is the distribution of goods to people in this country, which is the true object of British industry, thereby advantaged? As the prices fall by this method, so the amount of money to purchase also falls, and we are as badly off as before, with the added complication of the discontent evoked by the reduction of wages.
As previous speakers from this comer of the house have intimated, the social credit remedy is the creation of credit, and its distribution direct to the consumer, to make up for the chronic shortage of purchasing power. The answer to that, of course, by the orthodox, is inflation. I would like to read 
Douglas' remarks on inflation, because social crediters, and particularly Douglas, are spoken of as inflationists. This is what Douglas has to say on inflation:
There is almost nothing to be said for a policy of deflation, as defined by the average banker, except that it provides a breathing space in which to consider what to do; the real argument against it is not that it reduces prices, but that it only does so at the expense of the producer, but a policy of inflation, that is to say a policy of increasing issues of money or credit, in such a manner that it can only reach the general public through the medium of costs, and must therefore be reflected in prices, has one thing and one thing only to be said for it at this time; that it is absolutely and mathematically certain to reduce any financial and economic system to ruins. It is in fact a capital levy of the meanest and most one-sided description since it taxes the purchasing power of those who obtained it by work, for the benefit of those who obtain it by financial manipulation.
When we are warned about the terrible consequences of inflation, the German example is always pointed out to us. But our opponents always omit to say that the German inflation was deliberate, and was caused so as to destroy Germany's internal debt and, as they thought, to give her a better chance of paying her external debt. That was done deliberately. However, I do not know of any instance in British history, or the history of any other country, where inflation has brought about any real ruin. On the other hand, since the end of the war deflation has cost in the loss of real wealth infinitely more than the great war itself. I had a letter from Senator Thomas, who is the senator from Oklahoma and, I believe, chairman of the agriculture and forestry committee of the senate of the United States, in which he said that since 1929 it was calculated that' deflation in the United States had cost that country a loss of real wealth, that is, wealth which might have been produced but which was not, to the extent of 8250,000,000,000.
We learned more about finance during the four years of the great war than I suppose we would have learned in four hundred years of peace. How was it possible to finance the cost of the great war amounting to tens of thousands of millions of dollars without inflation? The answer is that during war time finance was put to its proper use and financiers were put in their proper places. In peace times those who are in control of the financial policies, namely private individuals and private corporations answerable to none but themselves, deliberately and designedly bring about conditions of inflation and deflation. In war times the financier is put in his proper place. He dare not bring about

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
such a condition for if it were known he would be put against the wall and shot. When we consider the misery that has been forced on the people of Canada during the last seven or eight years, then I say that those who caused it should be brought before the bar of this house and made to answer to this parliament for their crimes. When we do that, then we can say that this is a sovereign parliament.
It is a curious thing, but history is absolutely dumb on the questions of money and finance. I believe I had a reasonably fair education. I have spent a lifetime on the farm, but I have been always a heavy reader. I have read a lot of history, but I was fifty years of age before I knew anything about money. I do not mean knowledge of the manipulation or the accumulation of money; I mean knowledge of the nature of money. Until then I knew little more than I did when I went to school. A man could take the highest honours in any university and still know nothing of the fundamental part that money has played during the course of our history. We read of great famines and hard times down through the ages and in most cases governments and nature have been blamed. We realize now that it was nothing but financial manipulation. That was one of the great causes of bad times. As the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr.' Blackmore) said the other day, Edward III attempted to overcome this by debasing the currency. At that time the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) replied that Edward III was merely trying to get rich quick for his own benefit. I would remind the hon. member for New Westminster that Edward III lived before the conquest of England by Scotland.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: If you said that Scotland conquered England you would be correct.

speechtext: It was when William Patterson, a native of Dumfries, founded the Bank of England in 1694.

speechtext: Douglas never conquered Scotland.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
No; he reconquered England. Before I conclude I should like to remark that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) told us the other night that this government, or one might say, that he himself as Minister of Finance controlled the financial policy of Canada. One might as well say that a sultan's steward controls the sultan's harem, obviously the control is very remote. The house has heard Douglas's opinion of inflation, and I think it can be said that he is no more looking for inflation than is anybody else. He suggests a
simple way of preventing it. Inflation is not, as so many seem to think, an increase in the amount of money. It seems to me that many people do not know the difference between inflation and expansion. Inflation means an increase of money accompanied by an increase in prices.
The orthodox speak about the inexorable laws of economics; but there are no such laws, there are merely rules. You might as well talk about the laws of whist or bridge. These are merely rules made by men that can be altered by men any time they care to do so. If I drop this book it falls to the ground according to one of the inexorable laws of nature. There is no altering that law, but I do not think it is right to say that the rules of economics are laws. I have only to mention the gold standard. A few years ago it was regarded as an inexorable law and we all know what has happened to that. I believe the orthodox view of inflation is based upon orthodox principles or rules of political economy. I would like to quote from Ricardo's Principles of Political Economy as follows:
The natural price of labour is that price which is necessary to enable the labourers, one with another, to subsist and to perpetuate their race without either increase or diminution. It is, in practice, more likely to fall below, than to rise above, the subsistence level, but, after their privations have decreased their numbers, the market price of labour will rise to the natural price.
That is a "law" of economics. It is fairly obvious that our opponents regard any state of prosperity that is above or even a little below the subsistence level as inflation, and the only remedy they see, like the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) is to lower wages and purchasing power until the sufferings and privations of the labourers would cause a scarcity of labour and eventually a rise in its price. We do not see it in that way. We do not believe that is a law: we think it is a rule.
Douglas has provided a very simple way to avoid inflation. He suggests that retail prices be lowered to the extent necessary to equate production and consumption, and that then the retailer be compensated by the treasury for the amount which he would thus be out of pocket. That would prevent inflation because it starts out with a reduction in prices. In other words, Douglas proposes that the people be enabled to buy their retail goods at the real cost of production instead of at their financial cost. We say, and we prove-I have not the time to do so tonight-that the price of goods produced is,

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
or ought to be, the cost of goods consumed; in other words, that consumption is the cost of production.
The just price, or the price discount, whichever you like to call it, is not a fixed price. It does not attempt to set a price. It allows prices to find their natural level through the free play of competition, but it does say that whatever the retailers find it necessary to charge for their goods in order to pay for their production and provide the retailer with a living, that level shall be reduced until the total prices in the country equal the total amount of purchasing power in the consumers' pockets. That credit would be created by the state-not by taxes, of course. I do not know why some people imagine and will insist that the only source of money which a government has is what it can borrow or what it can raise by taxation, and if we have done nothing else since we have been here, we have at all events persuaded the Minister of Finance to admit that banks can and do create money. And if banks can do it, I would like to be told why the state itself cannot do it. But apparently the inexorable law of economics in some miraculous way prevents it. The banks can do it, but the state cannot.
The easiest way to understand the subject is perhaps from a short illustration. Here I would like to read a statement that was handed to me by the Douglas Social Credit Bureau of Canada, headed Production and Consumption. They wish me to make this statement for them:
In dealing with estimates or with actual figures of production and consumption, it is well to bear in mind that, for the most part, the statistics obtainable to-day are only approximately correct. They are sufficiently accurate, however, to permit definite conclusions to be reached.
The dominion bureau of statistics gives actual production in Canada for the year 1935 as 2,554 million dollars and consumption as 2,036 million dollars, or eighty per cent of actual production. There is, however, a vast difference between actual production and potential production, for whereas consumption may be eighty per cent of actual production, it might be a mere fifteen or twenty per cent of the potential production attainable if our enormous plant operated at full capacity.
The Rotary International social credit research committee-
The Rotary International set up a committee to inquire into social credit, and it brought in this report:
The Rotary International social credit research cotamittee in its report gave the following estimate:
"The present potential output of industry is at least four times its actual output."

Thus we have a picture of consumption being eighty per cent of actual production and, in turn, actual production being twenty-five per cent of estimated potential production.
Further, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics gives actual production for the boom year of 1928 as 4,122 million dollars and consumption for the depression year of 1933 as 1,777 million dollars, or forty-three per cent of the "proved capacity to produce" attained in 1928, which in turn was less than the potential capacity to produce.
No physical deterioration had occurred between 1928 and 1933 and the capacity of Canadians to consume had not altered but a financial collapse had restricted purchasing power. This illustrates the vast difference between demand and effective demand. The desire for goods and services, which is demand, counts for little without the necessary purchasing power to make it effective demand.
Considerable effort has been made in some quarters to link rising prices or inflation with social credit, in effect confusing one of the injurious processes of the present, financial system with its remedy. The Douglas price discount formula is a scientifically devised mechanism designed to act as a governor that will automatically prevent either inflation or deflation, maintaining a balance between supply on the one hand and effective demand on the other.
The Douglas Social Credit Bureau of Canada, Inc.,
Ralph L. Duclos,
President.
Suppose we take the figures which are quoted here, that according to the bureau of statistics consumption this year equalled eighty per cent of actual production. I have said that retail prices would be reduced to the point where consumption and production would equate, and this would mean that we could reduce the prices of retail goods by twenty or twenty-five per cent. That is to say that an article retailing at a dollar could be sold to the public for seventy-five cents, and the retailer would then be compensated by the treasury for the amount he was out of pocket. In that way, whatever the people cared to produce they would be enabled to consume, and industry would become for the first time self-liquidating, so that it would be possible to continue without incurring debt- which is certainly impossible to-day. I might go into the details of how that is to be administered, but I do not think it is necessary. There is the principle; it is designed to prevent inflation by stopping it before it starts, because it acts by means of reducing prices, and you cannot have inflation unless prices increase.
Social credit is a great deal more than a system of economics; it is a philosophy of government and a philosophy of life. Douglas says:
What are we trying to get? What are we aiming at? We are endeavouring to bring to birth a New Civilization. We are doing

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
something which really extends far beyond the confines of a change in the financial system. We are hoping, by various means, chiefly financial, to enable the community definitely to step out of one type of civilization into another type of civilization, and the first and basic requirement of that, as we see it, is absolute economic security.
Now, as to the social credit idea of government, we believe that it is the privilege of the people to demand what they want, to demand results, and it is the duty of their representatives to obtain those results for the people who elected them, not by turning themselves into amateur experts but by engaging the experts needed to do the technical work. I have heard that idea laughed at, but how else do we do a thing when we have to accomplish something really big? I was not a member of this house when war was declared ; but I am certain that hon. members did not then rise in this chamber and express their ideas of inflation and deflation and advise how this, that, and the other thing shoidd be done. They were not concerned with exactly how these things were to be done; what they said was, "They must be done," and they ordered those who were responsible to get them done, because they knew that if those objects were not achieved they would be answerable for their failure to the people. If that be true in time of war, why is it not true in time of peace? In war time anything physically possible becomes financially possible, but in peace time only what is financially desirable is permitted to become physically possible. As soon as we say that you could cure unemployment; that you could reduce the age for old age pensions to sixty or even fifty years and could pension the blind, the lame and the halt if you really wanted to do so, what do we hear? What have I heard repeatedly in this chamber? "Yes, of course it ought to be done, but where is the money coming from? We cannot afford it." I should like to see any hon. member, if war were declared next week, rise in the house and say, "We cannot go to war, Mr. Speaker, for where is the money to come from?"

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: How do you know that will not be done?

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext:
It never was done and
never will be done. A few years ago the people of Great Britain were faced with the consequences of unemployment and other social problems which occasioned great suffering; but no matter what was proposed by way of remedy, whether the dole, or widows' pensions, or mothers' allowances, or any other social service, always the objection was raised.
"Where is the money to come from?" When, however, it became evident to the real rulers of the nation that their own property and lives were in danger from enemy action, did anyone say, "How are we going to finance ten thousand million dollars to increase our defences?" I am not arguing against the expenditure of money upon defence. If you want to, you can spend up to the limit of your physical capacity to produce. What I do say, though, is that if money can be found for war it can be found for peace. If this house is a sovereign parliament, as it is said to be, the money can be found. Unfortunately the experts, who, of course, are the only people qualified to carry out policies, formulate the policies themselves. As Douglas says:
The experts should be on tap, not on top.
But that is where they are, all over the world. The financial expert is not so much on tap as he is on top. As Mr. McKenna says, bankers control the policies of governments and hold the destiny of the people in the hollow of their hands. The proof of this is that Canada, along with all other countries, was able to finance a great war. Before the outbreak of that war it was said that such a thing was impossible because there was not enough money to finance it. But the war did not stop for lack of money. Nobody ever said, "You cannot put these men into the firing line; you cannot pay them a dollar a day; we have not the money." The money was found; if there was any idea worth while it was carried out without reference to the money cost. And all this was done without any degree of inflation worth mentioning. There was prosperity in spite of the fact that the cream of the nation was either in the firing line or in the munition factories producing, not goods and services which the people needed, but shot and shell. Yet I repeat that in spite of these vast numbers engaged in munition factories or serving in the trenches, the mass of the people lived better during the war than they have ever lived, before or since. And the reason, the only reason, is that finance was put to its proper use and the financier put in his proper place. We have heard it said that the war impoverished the world, but it did nothing of the kind, apart from the appalling loss of life. In any material sense the world was infinitely richer after the war than before. The productive capacity of all countries was enormously increased. But having won the war we had to lose the peace. The financier lost it. What else could he do? It is an inexorable law that financial control by the financiers is absolutely certain to bring

Use oj Canada's Financial Resources
about the position we are in to-day of poverty and unemployment. It cannot do anything else; it is not meant to do anything else.
We believe that the people, and only the people, have the right to decide on policy. But the carrying out of that policy is the business of experts. Let me illustrate. Suppose a community wanted to build a bridge. They lived by a river and the only means they had of crossing was a ferry. As the papulation increased they found the ferry inconvenient so they began to consider the possibility of building a bridge.

speechtext: I am sorry to have to tell the hon. member that his time has expired.

speechtext: Might I finish this illustration.

speechtext: Go on.

maintopic: ELIMINATION OF POVERTY-AMENDMENT OF MR. BLACKMORE
speechtext: A meeting would be called to discuss the question of building a bridge. Now that question of whether the bridge should be built is entirely, for the public to decide. Having decided that, they would call an engineer to give an estimate of its cost. The engineer would say, "Well gentlemen, what kind of bridge do you want? Do you need a foot-bridge or a bridge for motor cars or one to carry Street cars and a railway?" That question having been settled, the engineer would examine the site, prepare plans and present them to the people, probably with an estimate of the cost. They would decide whether they were willing to spend that sum and, if so, would instruct the engineer to go ahead and build the bridge. The actual design of the bridge they would leave to the engineer, as an expert; he would be responsible for the design of the structure. That is what we mean when we say the people settle the policy and the experts carry it out. That is the policy of the Alberta government at the present time. Those men were elected to obtain results. I know many of the members of the Alberta legislature myself, some of them intimately. They are not here to speak for themselves, so I want to say something in their defence. I can speak for myself and you can judge me as you please; I do not care what you think of me. But, knowing these men, I say that no people were ever represented by a finer, more honest and hard working lot of representatives than the present members of the legislature of Alberta.

speechtext:
May I remind the house of the exact wording of the proposed amendment:
That all the words in the motion after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

This house is of the opinion that for the effective removal of poverty from Canada this government has neglected and is now neglecting to use the resources of the dominion as adequately as the people of this country have a right to demand.
I read that because I am going to deal first with what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has said and then follow that by attempting to show that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in his rebuttal did not attempt to refute the argument of the hon. member for Lethbridge. In fact one is tempted to think that the speech of the Minister of Finance was not prepared in any terms whatsoever as a rebuttal of the argument put forth in that debate. The Minister of Finance dealt a. good deal with w'hat the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) said a year ago and then launched into something of an attack upon the Douglas social credit philosophy.
The hon. member for Lethbridge dealt first with the question, What is money? He showed the difference between currency and credit, and used a term which, I think, was unique for this house at least, advocating " king-created " money. Of this the Minister of Finance made no particular mention The hon. member for Lethbridge then dealt with the sources of money, and contended that money is in the last analysis created. I should like to amplify that a little. When one talks of money there seems to be some little misunderstanding regarding its source. In fact while the hon. member for Lethbridge was speaking along this line and attempting to show that there was only one source from which money should come, an hon. member on the other side said, "Why, you can earn it." This did not get into Hansard, but the remark was heard by myself.
I should like to point out that there is a difference between the source from which money comes and the avenue through which it comes. Some months ago I was having a bit of an argument with a gentleman, and I asked him where money came from anyway. He said, "Why, if I have a farm out here and grow a crop of wheat, the money comes from my wheat." I said, "Well, sir, you do not mean to tell me that money actually grows on your land?" "Yes, yes; of course it does. That is it." For the life of me I could not seem to drill into that gentleman's mind that there was a difference between his receiving money by means of the sale of a crop of wheat, and the source from which money originally came.

Use of Canada's Financial Resources
I believe a year or two ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) raised the same question, and I know he is well informed upon this subject. At that time he suggested that all money comes through production. I think I am right in that reference, though I am trusting to my memory. It was either a year ago or two years ago. Of course the Minister of Labour was right in what he said; but I should like to point out to hon. members that if he had said that money comes from production he would have been wrong, and I think he is aware of that fact. In other words, that is a difference between money coming through the process of production and money originating with production. The hon. member for Lethbridge attempted to point this out. Money does not grow on trees. We do not dig it from the ground, and at its source we do not earn it. It is created by the banking system, and it gets out into circulation only by way of a primary loan. Whether or not all the hon. members are aware of this I do not know; but the result is that when loans are paid money is taken out of circulation, and I think it goes without saying that all the money which is in existence has a debt attached to it by reason of the fact that the only way it came into existence was through a primary or initial loan.
This argument the Minister of Finance neither confirmed nor denied. In the next place the hon. member for Lethbridge dealt with what gave money value. He said that in the first place it was confidence; that in the next place Canada was behind it as a nation, and that what gave value to money were the goods and services, the producing and consuming power of the nation. I think the minister would agree with that, although he did not touch it in his speech. The hon. member for Lethbridge then went on logically to discuss how much money Canada could have, and he showed that it all depends upon the use Canada can make of the money, that is upon the number of exchanges the people of Canada can be enabled to make. In this connection I am going to do some quoting, from Planned Money by Sir Basil Blackett, at pages 103 and 106. I hope my hon. friends opposite will not be too much discouraged when we give these quotations, though it is beginning to appear that citations from eminent authorities are a little bit annoying to them. This is the quotation:
The purchasing power of the medium of circulation depends solely on the relation between the quantity in which it is available and the work which it is at any given moment called upon to perform.
A few pages later this quotation occurs:
It is customary in most countries to place strict limits on the amount of notes which the central bank may issue. Such restrictions are usually bound up with laws and regulations regarding the amounts or proportions of the total issue which must be covered or backed by gold or particular kinds of securities, internal and external. There is no need for any such restrictions in the local currency system now under discussion-at any rate, in one which has no foreign contacts. The right amount of currency in circulation at any given moment is that amount which will do the work required of it at a given level of prices. If it is too much, prices will rise. If it is too little they will fall.
The next question my hon. friend asked was whether king-created money was sound. The Minister of Finance rather agreed with this, not in his speech but in some comments that he made at the time. Then my hon. friend went on to point out that the present financial set-up is such that for every dollar of gold which the Canadian banking system can create, eighty dollars of money-that is, four Bank of Canada bills and S76 in bank credit-can be issued. Here I should like to give a quotation from The Canadian Banking System, by Professor James Holladay, doctor of philosophy and professor of economics at the university of Alabama. This appears at page 140:
The Bank Act of 1934, however, sets up a specific quantitative reserve which tile chartered banks are required to hold against their deposit liabilities. In form, this reserve must consist of a deposit in and notes of the Bank of Canada. In amount, it must be equal to five per cent of the deposit liabilities in Canada. As a result, the chartered banks as a group can legally create deposits amounting to $20 on the basis of a one dollar reserve. A much larger secondary expansion is made possible, however, for the Bank of Canada is required to hold only a twenty-five per cent reserve against its liabilities, which in turn constitute the reserves of the chartered banks. Consequently, the Bank of Canada can expand a dollar into four dollars of liabilities which, if borrowed by the chartered banks, will enable them to lend an aggregate of $80 against a primary deposit of one dollar. This compares with a possible legal expansion of $28.50 under the federal reserve system in vogue in the United States.

phrases: One. "Down with Aberhart"; the other one, "Put good, sound business men in government." Turn for a moment to the history of "business" administration in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. The world to-day is a small world; people everywhere are turning their minds to the question of money. They recognize that it is the key position to the solution of many of our social evils. They know, as indeed any boy in kindergarten knows, that if a nation can produce plenty there should not be starvation. I wonder if they taught that in the Liberal school. Even an ass when he is hungry will not pass a pile of hay without taking a nibble; but human beings are deprived of that privilege; if they go into a restaurant and get a meal for which they have not the means of payment they are put in gaol and termed communists or classed with disreputable people. The thin shoulders of the poor snap back; they are the first to have a uniform; then they get a dollar ten a day and are treated as Canadians, taking their place in Canadian society.

To-day all the people of the British Commonwealth of Nations are turning their attention to this thing called money. They want to know the nature of it. History tells us that in the past most parliamentarians knew nothing of money, and the situation has not changed much since. Listen to men who have passed on, men who made great contributions to their country. For instance Thomas Jefferson said:
I believe that banking institutions are more dangerous to our liberties than standing armies. Already they have raised up a monied aristocracy that has set the government at defiance. The issuing power should be taken from the banks and restored to the people to whom it properly belongs.
F. G. Bonfils, former owner and editor of the Denver Post, said:
All gold produced in the world in 428 years would make a block thirty-eight feet square. Nearly two billion people are tied by the leg to this golden fetish.
Mr. S. P. Chase, secretary of the treasury from 1861 to 1864, chief justice of the United States supreme court from 1864 to 1873, said:
My agency in promoting the passage of the National Bank Act was the greatest financial mistake of my life. It has built up a monopoly which affects every interest in the country. It should be repealed; but before that can be accomplished the people will be arrayed on one side and the banks on the other, in a contest such as we have never seen before in this country.
Now let us review for a moment the latest campaign in the United States when seventy-five per cent of the press was against President Roosevelt because his battle was against money, a battle for the liberties of the people. With whom do we find the press aligning itself? Exactly the same thing happened in this country with social credit in Alberta. People who fight against the money power can expect no mercy and no justice from the press. I am glad to see that some men in the Canadian parliament have seen the difficulty which faces us. For instance, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said:
Canada on the dole is like a young and vigorous man in the poorhouse. The dole is a condemnation, final and complete, of our economic system. If we cannot abolish the dole we should abolish the system.

We find that money is the root of the whole thing. Splitting hairs over irrelevant matters will not bring us one step nearer the goal. It has been said by the leader of our group that we are not a political party; that we are an economic group. We believe that the duty of parliament is to call in experts to carry out the mandate given by the people. Parliament should place upon the statute books the necessary legislation to carry out the mandate of the people. Many people are taking an interest in monetary reform. Let us turn for a moment to the church; let me quote from a letter from the Very Rev. Paul Stacey, of Coventry, England:
In the past they have endeavoured to link the need for monetary reform with an understanding of Christian values, and to obtain united Christian support. This policy has caused many misunderstandings, but it is now generally realized that we have been working along the right lines.
Commenting on a statement issued by various churches concerning the need of monetary reform, a United Christian petition campaign is being started, and a petition to parliament prepared, similar to the petition to the king in council, to be used simultaneously in England and the dominions. The object of the parliamentary petition is to enable the dominions to bring pressure to bear upon their parliaments while cooperating in the empire petition to the king, and to enable Christian people in other countries to join in the united action by petitioning their legislative bodies and arousing public opinion. The relation between the monetary reformer and the Christian petition movement is obvious. The petition is an instrument for mobilizing public support which will enable the new economies to be given a fair trial. The statement of the various churches referred to maintains that:
The notion that our souls may find salvation whilst we are indifferent to the needs of our brethen whose souls are warped through living under evil social conditions, or, on the other hand, through amassing great wealth by methods injurious to their fellow' men-a condition contrary to Christian teaching and to common sense.
Widespread poverty in an age of abundance, and the inability of great nations to find employment for hundreds of thousands of their citizens-except when they are preparing for war-are the major symptoms of the general disorder.
One of the primary functions of the state is to safeguard and foster the material and

spiritual wellbeing of the individual and the home. As long as the state fulfils this function it is entitled to respect and has a rightful claim on our loyal allegiance.
The church must reject financial dictatorship, because it treats man as a machine, whereas in fact he is a child of God.
Under the leadership of the Pope and the Archbishop of York respectively, a group of leading men in both churches have declared that we must work to suppress the private monopoly of credit. And both are explicit as to the means and objective.
I could read dozens of quotations from prominent church people. When I spoke last in this house I challenged the ministers of the crown for just one hour in their busy lives to put aside their parliamentary duties and go and see how the other half lives. Go down to the soup kitchens; see these men shovelling snow for relief. The press accuses them of cheating and chiselling. It is a crime the way we are making cheats and chisellers of the poor. We make them sign an affidavit that they have not earned $2 outside their relief. A man has to choose between swearing a false affidavit or buying a child a pair of shoes, and like a Christian he swears the false affidavit and buys the shoes. I could go on and on, but I wonder whether anyone will ever rise in this house and make an impression upon the government as to what faces them. I wish hon. members would lose their incomes for a while; I wish they were cast adrift like thousands of Canadians; then they would get a more complete education in six weeks than they have had in the last twenty years.
The Minister of Finance, again speaking in Edmonton, told Alberta that if it voted against the Liberal party it would be a clear indication that it wanted to remain away from the other provinces. Well, just a moment; since when was there such unity among the Liberal governments of Canada? We find a motion introduced in the Manitoba legislature by Mr. Turnbull calling upon this government to bring about monetary reform, and that resolution was adopted. We find some disagreement between Mr. Duplessis and this government; we find some disagreement between Mr. Hepburn and this government, and I have a suspicion that even the members of the party in this house do not all agree.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I should like to say a few words about western Canada.
